extracted.intended_audience: graduate students / advanced undergraduates in algebraic geometry (Math 216)
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook section defining and developing core algebraic-geometry concepts: canonical bundle and geometric genus, plurigenera and Kodaira dimension, classes of varieties (Fano/Calabi-Yau/general type), Kodaira vanishing, Hodge numbers, unramified morphisms and ramification, the Riemann–Hurwitz formula, and the blow-up construction with its universal property and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical bundle KX (canonical sheaf, Ω^n_X/k = det Ω_X/k)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a smooth k-variety X of dimension n, the invertible sheaf det Ω_X/k = Ω^n_X/k (the sheaf of algebraic volume forms) is the canonical (invertible) sheaf or canonical (line) bundle, denoted KX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KX is the sheaf appearing in Serre duality (see Miracle 18.5.2) and is important for many invariants (geometric genus, pluricanonical maps); when X is projective KX is the dualizing sheaf ωX/k. The text points to later uses (e.g., adjunction formula, exercises) and connections with Serre duality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjunction formula for KX (exercise 21.5.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is smooth and Z ⊂ X is a smooth subvariety, there is an adjunction relation between KZ and KX involving the normal bundle: in codimension 1, KZ ∼= (KX ⊗ OX(Z))|Z (and more generally KZ ∼= KX|Z ⊗ det N_{Z/X}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: apply Exercise 13.5.H to Theorem 21.3.8; used inductively for complete intersections. The exercise and surrounding comments emphasize using adjunction repeatedly in computations of canonical bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric genus pg(X)
rubrics_metrics.description: For projective (or proper) smooth X, the birational invariant h^0(X, KX) = h^0(X, Ω^n_{X/k}) is the geometric genus pg(X). For irreducible varieties not smooth/projective, pg(X) refers to h^0(X', K_{X'}) for a smooth projective X' birational to X (well-defined by exercise 21.5.A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for curves the geometric genus coincides with topological and arithmetic genus (in characteristic 0 after Miracle 18.5.2). The text notes dependence on resolution of singularities in higher dimension and references Hironaka for characteristic 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurigenera and Kodaira dimension κ(X)
rubrics_metrics.description: The jth plurigenus is P_j(X) = h^0(X, K_X^{⊗ j}). The Kodaira dimension κ(X) is the smallest k such that h^0(X, K_X^{⊗ j})/j^k is bounded as j varies among positive integers; if all plurigenera are 0, κ(X) = −1. κ(X) is an integer between −1 and dim X and is a birational invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Kodaira dimension tracks growth of plurigenera; κ(X) = dim X means X is of general type. The text observes nontrivial facts (existence of κ and relation to pluricanonical rational maps) and refers to further literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Important classes of varieties: Fano, Calabi–Yau, general type
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (as used in the text): Fano, Calabi–Yau, and general type are important classes determined by properties of the canonical bundle/Kodaira dimension. Informally: Fano (anti-canonical positive/ample), Calabi–Yau (trivial canonical class in the usual sense), and general type (κ(X)=dim X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives exercises to test these definitions on curves (Exercise 21.5.G) and complete intersections (21.5.H, 21.5.I) and cautions about variant definitions. The trichotomy for curves (genus 0,1,>1 correspond to Fano, Calabi–Yau, general type respectively) is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kodaira Vanishing Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If k has characteristic 0 and X is a smooth projective k-variety, then for any ample invertible sheaf L, H^i(X, K_X ⊗ L) = 0 for i > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The characteristic 0 restriction is necessary (Raynaud counterexample in positive characteristic). Historical proof uses complex-analytic methods and Serre's GAGA; other approaches use Lefschetz principle or positive-characteristic techniques. Exercises show simple cases (dim X = 1, P^n) where characteristic restriction is not needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hodge numbers hi,j and Hodge diamond symmetries
rubrics_metrics.description: Define h^{i,j}(X) = dim H^j(X, Ω^i_{X/k}). For smooth projective X, certain symmetries hold: hi,0 are birational invariants; assuming Miracle 18.5.2 leads to Serre-duality symmetry h_{p,q} = h_{n-p,n-q}; over k = C there is Hodge decomposition H^m(X,C) = ⊕_{i+j=m} H^j(X, Ω^i_{X/C}) and complex-conjugation symmetry hi,j = hj,i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives Hodge-diamond examples (surfaces, P^n, curves), exercises to compute Hodge numbers of projective space and curves, and remarks about which Hodge numbers are birational invariants (hi,0 are, but not all hi,j). It notes that some symmetries can fail in positive characteristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitesimal deformations and automorphisms (tangent sheaf cohomology)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a variety X: H^0(X, T_X) parametrizes infinitesimal automorphisms of X; H^1(X, T_X) parametrizes infinitesimal deformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for X = P^1, T_{P^1} ≅ O(2) so h^0(P^1, T_{P^1}) = 3 equals dimension of automorphism group. Exercises compute h^i(C, T_C) for curves of genus g.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of unramified and formally unramified morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: For a morphism π: X → Y, the sheaf Ω_{π} = Ω_{X/Y} has support called the ramification locus. If Ω_{π} = 0, π is formally unramified; if furthermore π is locally of finite type (or locally of finite presentation in some references), then π is unramified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution about slight differences in the literature (finite type vs finite presentation). Many exercises provide examples (locally closed embeddings, finite separable field extensions) and properties (stability under composition, fiber characterizations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizations and basic properties of unramified morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalent fiberwise characterizations: π is unramified iff for each point q of Y, the fiber π^{-1}(q) is a disjoint union of Specs of finite separable extensions of κ(q); similar geometric-point version. Unramified morphisms are preserved under composition, and the locus where π is unramified is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises provide practice: normalization of nodes vs cusps, local criteria using diagonal embedding being a closed embedding, and number-theoretic version via finite-type local homomorphisms agreeing with classical unramified notion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different and discriminant (arithmetic remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: For rings of integers B over Z (or more generally), the different ideal is the annihilator of Ω_{B/Z}; it measures failure of Spec B → Spec Z to be unramified. The discriminant ideal is the pushforward to Spec Z of the different and measures branch locus arithmetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an arithmetic-side remark; the text does not use these ideas further here but points out the analogy with ramification locus and branch locus on schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ramification divisor and its local interpretation (curves)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite separable morphism of smooth curves π: X → Y, the ramification locus is a finite set of points of X and has associated ramification orders; in local DVR coordinates, if t (uniformizer on Y) pulls back to u s^n in A then dt vanishes to order at least n−1 giving the ramification order (tame vs wild).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.7.B: the degree of Ω_{X/Y} at p equals the ramification order. Exercise 21.7.C: in the tame case the branch divisor multiplicity at q equals deg π − |π^{-1}(q)|, interpreting how number of preimages falls short of degree. These local computations motivate the Riemann–Hurwitz formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of the branch locus for generically separable morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is generically separable between irreducible smooth varieties of same dimension n, then the relative cotangent sequence is left-exact and the ramification locus is pure codimension 1; locally it is cut out by the determinant (Jacobian) of the n×n map of differentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement is proposition 21.7.2 and exercise 21.7.A; it is a special case of Zariski's theorem on purity of the branch locus. The text explains interpreting the determinant of the Jacobian as the local equation for the ramification divisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Hurwitz formula (for curves)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is a finite separable morphism of projective regular curves of degree n and R is the ramification divisor, then 2g(X) − 2 = n(2g(Y) − 2) + deg R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21.7.D suggests proof via exact sequence (21.7.2.1) and additivity of degree; applications include parity of deg R (always even), impossibility of certain maps between curves of given genera, Lüröth's theorem, bounds on automorphism groups (Hurwitz theorem), and counting discriminant degree. Many exercises connect the formula to concrete consequences and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and applications of Riemann–Hurwitz
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications discussed include: deg R is even; nonexistence of nonconstant maps from genus 2 to genus 3 curves; uniqueness of connected unbranched finite separable covers of P^1 over algebraically closed fields of characteristic 0; Lüroth's theorem (subfields of k(x) containing k are k(f(x))); bounds on automorphism groups of curves (Hurwitz: |Aut(C)| ≤ 84(g − 1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 21.7.E–21.7.M walk through these consequences; the text outlines arguments using Riemann–Hurwitz and arithmetic of ramification indices to maximize group orders and deduce Hurwitz bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up: motivating example and geometric picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Blowing up the origin in A^2: Bl_{(0,0)} A^2 = { (p, ℓ) ∈ A^2 × P^1 : p ∈ ℓ } given algebraically by xY − yX = 0 in A^2 × P^1; projection to A^2 is an isomorphism off the origin, and the fiber over the origin is P^1 (the exceptional divisor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation: blowing up separates branches of a curve singular at the origin (proper/strict transform) and can partially desingularize; the construction generalizes to blowing up the origin in A^n (subset of A^n × P^{n−1} given by xi Xj − xj Xi = 0) and to blowing up regular subvarieties. The example illustrates smoothness, exceptional divisor as effective Cartier divisor, and projectivity of the blow-up morphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up defined by universal property
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a closed subscheme Y ↪ X (finite-type ideal sheaf), the blow-up Bl_X Y fits into a fiber diagram with exceptional divisor E_{X/Y} the scheme-theoretic pullback of Y which is an effective Cartier divisor on Bl_X Y, and Bl_X Y is universal for this property: any other such diagram with an effective Cartier divisor factors uniquely through Bl_X Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This universal-property definition is followed by an explicit construction in later sections; advantages and disadvantages of starting with the universal property are discussed. Exercises and subsequent sections develop consequences (existence, projectivity) and show equivalence with explicit constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit constructions and computations for blow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit affine/projective coordinate descriptions (e.g., equations xY − yX = 0) allow concrete computations: verifying smoothness via projections, describing the exceptional divisor, computing strict transforms of subvarieties, and checking that the blow-up morphism is projective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook emphasizes two complementary perspectives: the universal property (conceptual) and the explicit construction (computational). Later sections (22.3–22.4) prove existence and give many explicit computations and examples to illustrate behavior and applications (resolutions of singularities, desingularization of plane curves, etc.).
